title: Sats falling, murmur gone
objective: Recognize thrombosis risk in congenital heart disease and treat sudden loss of a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt as an emergency
secondaryObjectives: Explain why right-to-left shunting in cyanotic defects barely responds to supplemental oxygen, and the risks of chronic hypoxemia such as polycythemia, thrombosis and stroke

brief.situation: 13:00 in the pediatric cardiac ICU. You are the nurse for Theo, 7 weeks old, with pulmonary atresia, who had a modified Blalock-Taussig shunt placed at 10 days. He was admitted this morning with two days of vomiting and diarrhea; his usual saturation is 78-82%.
handover: At 08:00 his saturation was 79% with a loud continuous shunt murmur. IV fluids are running at maintenance as ordered.
He has had few wet diapers. At 12:50 his monitor started reading in the low 60s.

Unit policy: the nurse gives oxygen and an ordered isotonic fluid bolus for poor perfusion, and calls the cardiac intensivist at once for a fall in saturation from baseline or loss of the shunt murmur; anticoagulation, cardiology, the surgeon and ECMO are activated by the intensivist.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Why is Theo's saturation falling, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: A shunt-dependent infant with saturation far below baseline and a fading shunt murmur has shunt obstruction until proven otherwise; dehydration and polycythemia raise thrombosis risk, and supplemental oxygen barely helps a lesion with too little pulmonary flow.
parts.modelAnswer: He depends on that shunt for lung blood flow, he's way below his baseline, and the murmur's almost gone. He's dry and his hematocrit is 56, so he's set up to clot it. Oxygen won't do much.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Gives oxygen and the ordered fluid bolus, does not hold fluids or wait on the probe, and calls the cardiac intensivist at once for anticoagulation and cardiology, surgery and ECMO.
parts.modelAnswer: Oxygen on, give the fluid bolus, don't hold fluids or fiddle with the probe, and call the cardiac intensivist right now.

scoring.modelReasoning: A Blalock-Taussig shunt should keep its flow murmur. Loss of the murmur with profound hypoxia relative to baseline means shunt obstruction: an emergency treated with anticoagulation and a catheter or surgical procedure, with ECMO ready. Dehydration and polycythemia from chronic hypoxemia raise thrombosis risk; oxygen barely improves a cyanotic lesion with too little pulmonary blood flow. Give oxygen and the ordered fluid bolus, do not hold fluids, and call the cardiac intensivist at once.

o2Q.ask: While he goes to the lab: why did oxygen barely help?

choices.label: Too little blood reaches the lungs, so more oxygen in the lungs adds little
His lungs are full of fluid

o2Q.explain: With little pulmonary blood flow through a failing shunt, supplemental oxygen barely changes saturation; restoring flow is the treatment.
